We uncover that the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) locus harbors the most HSCA in immune cells, where we resolve specific transcription factor (TF) binding events disrupted by disease-associated variants. Finally, we demonstrate that the regulatory landscape of a cell is littered with autosomal somatic chromatin epimutations that are propagated by clonal expansions to create mitotically stable and non-genetically deterministic chromatin alterations.

articles.title: Comprehensive benchmarking of somatic mutation detection by the SMaHT Network.
articles.abstract: NA: Somatic mosaicism is increasingly recognized as a fundamental feature of human biology, yet the detection of somatic mutations remains challenging. The Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues (SMaHT) Network conducted large-scale benchmarking experiments involving cell lines and donor tissues to evaluate sequencing technologies, experimental approaches, and computational methods for detecting different types of somatic mutations, generating community resources with >1,000× short-read and 100-400× long-read data for nine analyzed samples. We determined effective strategies for utilizing short- and long-read sequencing for mutation detection and demonstrated that using donor-specific and pangenome-inferred diploid assemblies improved calling, extending mutation catalogs to challenging genomic regions. We benchmarked six duplex technologies and showed that single-cell sequencing resolves cell-type-specific mutational patterns and heterogeneity. Our results indicate that bulk, single-cell, and duplex analyses are complementary and that leveraging all three provides comprehensive characterization of mosaicism within tissues. Together, these findings provide the scientific and clinical communities with a roadmap for accurate genome-wide somatic mutation analysis.

articles.title: Charting the silent variation within us.
articles.abstract: NA: Every cell in the human body carries its own genome, shaped by mutations acquired over a lifetime, yet this vast somatic variation has been nearly impossible to measure. The SMaHT Network now delivers benchmarked tools and the first body-wide map of somatic mosaicism, establishing a baseline of "normal" against which its roles in development, aging, and disease can finally be tested.

articles.title: Cellular scaling laws in the mammalian brain.
articles.abstract: NA: Recent whole-brain cell atlases have uncovered a consistent cytoarchitectural feature: the greatest diversity of discrete neuronal cell types resides not in the regions with the most neurons (e.g., the cortex and cerebellum) but rather in deep subcortical structures like the hypothalamus and brain stem. We propose that this discrepancy reflects a fundamental algorithmic division in the vertebrate brain between a "learning subsystem" and a "steering subsystem." The learning subsystem (cortex, striatum, and cerebellum) scales via the replication of repetitive modules to maximize computational capacity, analogous to scaling up parameters in machine learning models. By contrast, the steering subsystem (hypothalamus, pallidum, and brainstem) scales via diversification of bespoke cell types to encode innate drives and reflexes, functioning as a high-dimensional biological "reward function." This framework explains the divergence in how evolution has influenced these subsystems and offers a unified lens for understanding brain architecture and the etiology of brain disease; furthermore, it may inform model designs for artificial intelligence.

articles.title: Milking the niche: Microbial control of neonatal hematopoiesis.
articles.abstract: NA: In this issue of Cell, Howard et al. reveal how the milk glycoprotein osteopontin shapes the neonatal microbiome to regulate hematopoiesis, promoting dendritic cell development and protection from severe respiratory infection. These findings uncover a maternal milk-microbiota pathway linking early-life nutrition to immune development and long-term disease susceptibility.

articles.title: A pseudoenzyme sensor of trehalose-6-phosphate directly represses the metabolic integrator SnRK1 in plants.
articles.abstract: NA: Trehalose-6-phosphate (T6P) is a central metabolic signal linking sugar availability to plant growth, carbon utilization, and productivity, yet its sensing and signaling mechanisms remain elusive. Using chemical biology and functional approaches, we identify the noncatalytic pseudoenzyme Class-II T6P synthase (TPS-II) as a T6P sensor in Arabidopsis. In the apo state, TPS-II dimerizes to form an autoinhibitory inter-subunit interaction. T6P binding to the N-terminal TPS-like domain triggers a conformational change that releases the C-terminal domain, enabling interaction with the central metabolic integrator SNF1-related protein kinase 1 (SnRK1) to repress its kinase activity. Loss of TPS-II genes activates catabolic and stress-responsive programs while suppressing anabolic gene expression, consistent with constitutive SnRK1 activity. Conservation of this T6P-TPS-II-SnRK1 signaling axis throughout the plant kingdom highlights its fundamental role in coupling carbon availability to metabolic homeostasis. These findings resolve a long-standing question in sugar signaling and provide a framework for improving crop carbon-use efficiency.
